newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO, EU hope for eased Greek-Turkish relations.
newsitem.headline: NATO, EU hope for eased Greek-Turkish relations.

text.p: NATO and the European Union, weary of years of Greek-Turkish bickering, looked on Monday for signs that Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis's election win would lead to an easing of tension in the eastern Mediterranean.

Diplomats and officials said that with an unequivocal victory under his belt, Simitis should be in a stronger position to bring Athens closer to Ankara after years of antagonism that has threatened security on the Western Alliance's flank.
"(NATO countries) clearly hope that there will be an amelioration as a result of the election," said one diplomat at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
Simitis's socialist party on Sunday won some 162 seats in the 300-seat parliament, giving him a solid majority and cementing his position as leader.

Western diplomats in Brussels said that Simitis, in contrast to his predecessor Andreas Papandreou, had already shown a desire to smooth things over with Turkey but had been somewhat strapped by an uncertain position at home.
"(We) feel he was being more helpful than Papandreou," the NATO diplomat said.
EU officials said the election win could give both Simitis and the 15-nation bloc room to manoeuvre.
"Certainly before the elections EU leaders were cautious about moving ahead on sensitive items (relating to Turkey)," one diplomat said.
"Simitis's election now gives a hope -- which may be fulfilled -- that Greece will be a little bit more flexible on EU relations with Turkey and relations with Cyprus," he said.

Greece has long blocked EU dealings with Turkey, notably a customs union to open lucrative EU markets to Turkish goods. Athens lifted its block only after a deal was reached under which Cyprus was given a date by which EU membership negotiations would begin.
Charging that Turkey is not living up to its side of the bargain and being a good neighbour, Greece has since held up financing to go along with the customs union.

Though infuriating many of its partners, it has received some support, notably from the European Parliament which said last week that it would block funding to Ankara because of allegations of human rights abuses.
But if the EU has mainly been concerned that Greek-Turkish tensions are hampering its economic ties with Turkey, the worry for NATO is that two of its members have come close to blows.
Passions between the two sides almost boiled over earlier this year in a dispute over unihabited islets in the Aegean.
The United States brokered a deal that defused the situation, but the two NATO allies remain very much at odds over their borders.
"It is of great concern to all of the allies that there is this festering situation between Greece and Turkey," a NATO diplomat said.
